beats.title: A dependency is a reason to wait
beats.outcome: Construct a task graph whose publication requires the right evidence.
beats.explanation: An orchestrator coordinates work; it does not invent its correctness rules. A [[dbxfe-orchestration-dependencies-concept|dependency]] tells Publish to wait for resolution and reconciliation. Independent inputs may run in parallel, but “finished” is not always “succeeded.” Write the condition next to the edge so a quality failure cannot accidentally flow into a current report.

handbook.markdown:
Draw the smallest graph that exposes business dependencies. A trigger starts work. A task performs a unit of work. An edge states when a dependent task can run. In our quality flow, raw retention precedes source resolution; publication also needs reconciliation and a true policy gate. Diagnostic recording may run on a failure branch.

Consider a flow configured to run Publish when upstream tasks are merely complete. That can include a failed quality check. The graph is syntactically valid but semantically unsafe for the intended report. Read run-if behavior deliberately and test the failure branch, not only the happy path.

Product Jobs orchestration is distinct from our local Python simulation. The simulation helps inspect state boundaries without a workspace. It does not validate a real job configuration, scheduler service or alert integration. In a real design record each task’s input contract, output location, idempotency behavior, timeout/retry owner and recovery evidence. A green task reports its configured success condition; the business check still needs to be meaningful.

beats.recap: The graph must encode business prerequisites, not merely a sequence of boxes.
beats.changeNote: New teacher-first explanation and worked visual; earlier lesson completion does not complete this beat.

beats.title: Four boundaries leave four kinds of evidence
beats.outcome: Locate what is durable or visible at an explicit failure point.
beats.explanation: Retained raw, resolved candidate, published snapshot and simulated effect are separate boundaries. A failure after one does not erase it automatically. Name the [[dbxfe-orchestration-boundaries-concept|failure boundary]] before choosing a retry. “The job failed” is insufficient: it does not tell you which input, report or effect already exists and which must be reconciled.

handbook.markdown:
Failure messages summarize process execution, not a complete transaction across every system. A process may retain input before crashing. It may publish a report before losing the response. It may send an external effect before recording the acknowledgment. A useful runbook identifies those boundaries explicitly.

Our local reference deliberately offers named failures after retained_raw, resolved_state and published_snapshot. It stores raw evidence, resolution state, the current/previous snapshot and a simulated outbox in one inspectable Python object. This lets the learner predict exactly what remains. It is not a durable distributed system: process loss, network retries and external recipients require additional design.

Before a recovery attempt record the last verified report identity, accepted row revisions, totals, coverage, conflict evidence and known effect keys. After recovery compare each against independent expected results. Do not call a candidate report current while the gate is false, and do not label an already published report absent merely because a later action failed. The next two beats move the same correction across different failure points.

beats.recap: A failed process can have successful earlier effects; inspect the boundary ledger.
beats.changeNote: New teacher-first explanation and worked visual; earlier lesson completion does not complete this beat.

beats.title: Recover after retaining the correction
beats.outcome: Predict recovery from raw evidence without duplicating business state.
beats.explanation: The baseline report is 20/1. A valid A3=14/1 correction is retained, then the run fails before resolution. The old report becomes stale_previous. Recovery reads the retained evidence, resolves A3+C to 22/1, and publishes only if the gate permits it. [[dbxfe-orchestration-raw-failure-concept|idempotency]] is checked on rows, totals, snapshot identity and effects, not on the raw arrival count.

samajh.text: Parcel receive ho gaya, par register update se pehle kaam ruk gaya. Dobara start karte waqt parcel mangwane se pehle dekho received evidence kya hai. Same correction ko do baar business total mein jodna nahi. Recovery ka matlab bache hue kaam ko trustworthy state tak le jana hai.
samajh.mapping: Received evidence survives before later bookkeeping completes.
samajh.boundary: The toy object is not a durable multi-system transaction or delivery service.

handbook.markdown:
Compute the expected result before recovering. The accepted business keys are A and C. A’s replacement rises from 12 to 14; C remains 8. The new total is 22 inspected and 1 defective. B’s nonconflicting baseline exclusion remains disclosed. The old 20/1 report is visible only as previous evidence while recovery is incomplete.

The canonical example below imports the retained-history pipeline and deliberately injects the named failure. It asserts the stale previous snapshot, recovery totals and replay behavior. These exact statements belong to the preserved locally executed exercise; opening this page or stepping the visual does not execute them.

If a conflicting payload also arrived, the expected outcome would change: recovery would preserve stale_previous and withhold publication. A retry must re-evaluate the gate, not assume the valid correction guarantees permission. In a production runbook, retain durable input references and compare all boundary outputs. The toy’s in-memory object explains the logic but does not promise process-crash durability.

~~~python
import json
from solutions.reference import LocalPipeline

with open("fixtures/baseline.json", encoding="utf-8") as handle:
    baseline = json.load(handle)
with open("fixtures/batches.json", encoding="utf-8") as handle:
    correction = json.load(handle)["correction"]
pipeline = LocalPipeline()
pipeline.ingest(baseline)
old_id = pipeline.published["snapshot_id"]
try:
    pipeline.ingest(correction, fail_after="retained_raw")
except RuntimeError:
    pass  # Expected injected failure only, not a general error suppression policy.
assert pipeline.status == "stale_previous"
assert pipeline.published["totals"]["inspected_units"] == 20
pipeline.recover()
assert pipeline.published["totals"]["inspected_units"] == 22
assert pipeline.published["totals"]["defective_units"] == 1
assert pipeline.published["snapshot_id"] != old_id
pipeline.recover()
assert len(pipeline.outbox) == 2  # One local effect per distinct published snapshot.
~~~

**Backfill is the same reasoning over a chosen past range.** A backfill reruns resolution for periods that already ran, for example after a late correction or a repaired rule. Bound the range by retained durable input, not by whatever files happen to be present; resolve each period with the same rules and the same publication gate; key every effect by snapshot identity so a period whose content did not change adds no second notification; and reconcile rows, totals and coverage per period against an independent ledger before calling the backfill complete. A backfill that silently re-publishes an unchanged period, or that relabels an older partial candidate as current, has repeated the failure this module exists to prevent.

beats.title: A published report is not undone by a later failure
beats.outcome: Recover an effect gap without publishing a duplicate business result.
beats.explanation: Move the failure after published_snapshot. The 22/1 report now exists, but its simulated effect may not. Recovery must recognize the already published snapshot and fill the missing effect once. A [[dbxfe-orchestration-published-failure-concept|snapshot identity]] connects the result to its effect record. Do not roll the explanation back to 20/1 just because the enclosing task reports failure.

handbook.markdown:
Separate the report state from the execution envelope. A failure after publication says the task did not finish every step; it does not say the report transaction or local publication assignment disappeared. Inspect the snapshot identity and content before deciding what remains.

In the local model, the snapshot identifier is derived from canonical business content and coverage. Recovery of identical evidence produces the same identity. The simulated outbox uses that identity as a key, so recording the same notification intent again does not create another entry. An A3 correction legitimately creates a new identity relative to the A2 baseline.

This is deliberately narrower than exactly-once email or webhook delivery. A real dispatcher can fail after sending but before recording acknowledgment; the receiver may need idempotency support, and the system needs a durable outbox and a retry protocol. The exercise sends nothing. Keep this limit in a customer explanation: we have tested local business-state/effect-key behavior, while real transport acknowledgment remains a separate validation requirement. The next beat makes that gap explicit.

beats.recap: Recover the missing boundary; do not pretend a completed publication never happened.

beats.title: A retry is not exactly-once delivery
beats.outcome: Explain the acknowledgment gap for an external side effect.
beats.explanation: An [[dbxfe-orchestration-effects-concept|outbox]] separates a business result from the intent to notify someone about it. The local exercise records one intent per snapshot; it sends no messages. A real sender could deliver, lose the acknowledgment, and retry. That gap needs a receiver/idempotency strategy and evidence. A successful data write alone cannot prove exactly-once external delivery.

samajh.text: Dost ko paisa bheja, app par “sending…” dikhta raha aur phir network chala gaya. Bank ne shayad transfer kar diya, shayad nahi. Dobara bhejoge toh double ja sakta hai; nahi bhejoge toh dost ko kuch nahi mila. Isliye har transfer ka ek reference number hota hai, aur bank usi number se pehchaan leta hai ki yeh wahi transfer hai. Outbox ka stable key waisa hi reference hai, lekin bank ki taraf ka duplicate check alag responsibility hai.
samajh.mapping: The stuck “sending” screen is the lost acknowledgment; the reference number is the stable intent key; the bank’s duplicate check is receiver-side idempotency.
samajh.boundary: A payment network provides reconciliation guarantees that a custom notification sink does not have unless you build and test them.

handbook.markdown:
Name the effect before discussing reliability: a table update, report pointer, email, webhook or payment are different operations with different acknowledgment behavior. The local outbox is an educational dictionary of intent, not a real notification service. Its stable key demonstrates one useful part of retry design.

Imagine a sender contacts a receiver, the receiver accepts, and the response is lost. From the sender’s perspective the result is unknown. Retrying without a deduplication key can repeat the effect; refusing to retry can lose an effect that never arrived. A durable intent, delivery attempts, receiver behavior and reconciliation policy are needed to handle that uncertainty deliberately.

Lakeflow Jobs repair reruns task logic; it does not make that logic idempotent. Likewise custom foreachBatch sink code must account for its own duplicate-write behavior. Product processing guarantees need a clearly named boundary and supported sink context. Avoid saying “exactly once” without naming what happens once and under which assumptions. Our exercise only establishes local repeatability of business snapshots and simulated effect records.

beats.recap: A stable intent key helps, but external acknowledgment is a separate reliability problem.
beats.changeNote: New teacher-first explanation and worked visual; earlier lesson completion does not complete this beat.

beats.title: A checkpoint belongs to a query
beats.outcome: Explain why deleting or sharing checkpoint state changes recovery semantics.
beats.explanation: A [[dbxfe-orchestration-checkpoint-concept|streaming checkpoint]] records progress and state for one query. It is different from a table-log checkpoint or a last-known dashboard total. Deleting it or switching locations starts fresh behavior; sharing it between queries is unsafe. Before restarting changed logic, check whether its sources, state and sink remain compatible with that checkpoint.

handbook.markdown:
A streaming checkpoint can contain source offsets, committed micro-batch information, stateful operator data and query identity. Those records connect a restart to a particular query’s earlier execution. A table-log checkpoint instead summarizes table metadata. The word checkpoint does not make these interchangeable.

When changing query logic, inspect the documented restart compatibility. A new filter may have different semantics even if technically restartable; a changed state schema or source/sink arrangement can require a different approach. Current runtimes include additional source-evolution mechanisms with specific requirements, so do not apply a universal “all changes are safe” or “all changes are impossible” rule.

Deleting progress to get past an error can replay data or change coverage. Before any such real action, preserve evidence and establish the desired reprocessing policy, destination behavior and reconciliation test. The local retained-history exercise has no real Structured Streaming checkpoint and makes no source-offset guarantee. It recomputes tiny stored Python evidence to teach state boundaries. That distinction keeps the illustrative code from becoming an accidental production runbook.

beats.recap: Query progress/state is a named recovery artifact with compatibility constraints.
beats.changeNote: New teacher-first explanation and worked visual; earlier lesson completion does not complete this beat.

beats.title: Green is a task result, not a business conclusion
beats.outcome: Compare post-recovery business outputs with an independent ledger.
beats.explanation: After recovery, compare accepted keys and revisions, totals, exclusions, conflicts, publication identity/status and simulated effects. A task can finish successfully while publishing the wrong population. [[dbxfe-orchestration-reconcile-concept|recovery reconciliation]] is the evidence that connects execution back to the customer’s decision. Keep a failed criterion visible even when other checks pass.

handbook.markdown:
Build the recovery ledger before running a retry. It should be independent of the implementation under test: for A3=14/1 and C1=8/0, explicitly expect 22/1, not a total computed by the same resolver function and then compared with itself. Include absence of duplicate keys and the correct report status.

If conflict evidence exists, the expected result is a blocked new report and a preserved stale previous snapshot, not successful publication. If no prior snapshot exists, expect blocked_no_snapshot. If the failure occurred after publication, expect the new report to remain and only the missing simulated effect to be completed. The boundary changes the expectation.

When a check fails, retain inputs, code/configuration version, relevant task errors and safe diagnostic output. Identify the responsible owner and smallest next test. A real Jobs repair uses current task settings, so record configuration changes that could affect comparison. Do not erase failed-run evidence after a green repair. This is an original runbook pattern, not an official incident procedure or proof of service availability.

beats.recap: Accept a recovery only after the intended business ledger reconciles.
beats.changeNote: New teacher-first explanation and worked visual; earlier lesson completion does not complete this beat.

beats.title: An order line changes the grain
beats.outcome: Transfer ordering/replay policy to a composite key and explicit cancellation.
beats.explanation: The transfer fixture uses (order_id, line_id), integer cents and explicit cancellation. O7/L1 is corrected to 3×300=900; O7/L2 is cancelled; O8/L1 contributes 2×200=400. The total is 1300 cents. The [[dbxfe-orchestration-transfer-concept|composite key]] prevents different lines from overwriting each other, while the cancellation remains current evidence rather than disappearing silently.

handbook.markdown:
Transfer the reasoning, not the inspection field names. First define the new grain: one current state per order line. The key has two fields, so O7/L1 and O7/L2 must coexist. Revisions still replace prior states within a key. Prices are integer cents to keep the worked arithmetic explicit; this is not a full currency/tax accounting system.

The current O7/L1 state has quantity 3 and unit price 300, contributing 900 cents. O7/L2 has an explicit cancellation tombstone with quantity 0, contributing zero while remaining traceable. O8/L1 contributes 400. Reconciliation expects three current rows, one cancelled, two active, order totals 900 and 400, and aggregate 1300. Omitting O7/L2 from a later incremental batch would not independently establish cancellation.

The preserved complete transfer solution and independent fixture exercise corrections, replay, composite identity and explicit deletion meaning. No order or payment is sent. A valid transfer answer names the changed key and operation contract, rather than blindly copying an inspection resolver and treating every absent line as deleted. Use the linked canonical cards to retrieve the boundary rules, then compare your own recovery ledger.

beats.recap: Recovery principles transfer only after the new grain, ordering and operation rules are explicit.

extensionCards.prompt: Does repair resume a failed task at its last Python line?
extensionCards.answer: No. The documented repair reruns the unsuccessful task from the beginning.
extensionCards.explanation: Partial outputs can already exist. Review what the task wrote and make repeat execution safe for its intended effects; a repair feature does not itself make task code idempotent.
extensionCards.whyItMatters: Prevents duplicate output after an apparently convenient retry.

extensionCards.prompt: A downstream publication task reads a missing validation key with a default of true. What risk does that create?
extensionCards.answer: The default can turn a missing or misnamed validation output into apparent permission to publish.
extensionCards.explanation: Suppose Validate intends to emit publication_allowed, but Publish requests publication_allow and supplies true as its default. A wiring error can look like an accepted gate. The documentation discourages defaults because they can conceal missing keys or incorrect task names. For this fictional gate, treat unavailable evidence as an explicit failure and investigate the task/key contract; that fail-closed policy is our design choice. [[dbxfe-orchestration-extension-task-values-concept|Task values]] are small metadata, not a replacement for a dataset: values must be valid JSON within 48 KiB. Pass a count, result status or approved output reference, while retaining substantive evidence in its proper destination. No job or data transfer is executed here.
extensionCards.whyItMatters: A dependency finishing does not prove its validation evidence reached the consumer.

extensionCards.prompt: A stateful foreachBatch callback only displays two rows and returns. Why might the next batch fail?
extensionCards.answer: It may leave the batch unconsumed; the documented stateful-query contract requires complete consumption or a restart.
extensionCards.explanation: A callback can return without having evaluated all of its DataFrame. In a hypothetical stream with watermark-based deduplication, displaying two rows is a preview, not evidence that the whole micro-batch completed. The documented stateful-query behavior requires [[dbxfe-orchestration-extension-full-consumption-concept|full consumption]] and can fail the next batch when it is missing. Design the callback so its intended work consumes the batch, and retain or propagate failures according to the recovery policy. Consuming rows is still different from verifying that the right business output was published. Do not introduce unbounded collect as a universal repair. This explanation adds a stateful streaming constraint; the course's in-memory recovery simulation does not exercise it.
extensionCards.whyItMatters: A successful-looking preview can hide incomplete stateful processing.

extensionCards.prompt: A cleanup task uses All done, but every dependency is Excluded. Is cleanup guaranteed to run?
extensionCards.answer: No. The documented all-dependencies-excluded rule excludes the cleanup task too.
extensionCards.explanation: An [[dbxfe-orchestration-extension-excluded-chain-concept|excluded task]] did not perform its work. Imagine a conditional branch that skips both inspection and correction tasks because the branch is not selected. A downstream cleanup task depends only on those two and uses All done. The documented exclusion rule still skips cleanup; All done is not an unconditional finally block. Before relying on cleanup or diagnostic publication, test successful, failed, cancelled and excluded branches separately and identify which branch actually owns the required action. Do not equate a missing cleanup record with successful cleanup. This is an original hypothetical job graph, not an executed Jobs run; actual cancellation and disabled-task behavior needs its own documented review.
extensionCards.whyItMatters: A recovery plan can silently omit its cleanup when the branch never ran.

recap.title: Recover the boundary that remains
recap.markdown:
**Inspect retained evidence → resolve again → check gate → reconcile publication → reconcile effects.** A checkpoint is query state; a green task is execution evidence. Use the current report label honestly and retain the previous snapshot when required.

**Next learning action:** Track B ends here; continue with C1 Data modeling and metric contracts (`#/module/dbxfe-modeling`), where the business grain these recoveries protect becomes an explicit model.

appliedTask.title: Failure after publication, then replay
appliedTask.prompt: A valid correction changes 20/1 to 22/1. Fail after published_snapshot and before the new simulated outbox entry, then recover twice. Predict the report, status and effect entries; explain why this proves no real notification guarantee.
appliedTask.modelAnswer: The 22/1 snapshot already exists with current_with_exclusions status. First recovery records its one missing effect key; second recovery adds no duplicate. The baseline key remains. This proves local keyed intent behavior only; no external notification is sent or acknowledged.
appliedTask.reasoning: The publication boundary succeeded before the failure. Recovery must complete the effect boundary without fabricating a rollback or a transport guarantee.
